title: Poppies
labelText: A summer field near Argenteuil, where Monet settled after the war of 1870. A woman and child — very likely Camille Monet and their son Jean — come down through the grass twice, once at the crest of the slope and again in the foreground, so that the eye walks the hillside with them. The poppies take the left half of the picture: pure vermilion, dabbed larger than life the nearer they come, dissolving botany into vibration. Shown at the first impressionist exhibition of 1874, the year the movement got its name.
extendedNote:
Argenteuil, on the Seine a quarter of an hour from the Gare Saint-Lazare, was where impressionism spent its happiest decade, and this small canvas is one of the reasons the word still smells of summer. Monet moved there in 1871 and painted the town's gardens, regattas and fields with a lightness he never quite recovered later. Here the subject is nothing at all: a slope of grass gone red with wild poppies, a line of trees closing the horizon, a sky of moving cloud, a walk taken twice.

The doubling is the picture's quiet machinery. At the top of the rise a woman with a parasol and a child stand against the sky; at the bottom right of the slope they appear again — the same pair, a minute later — the mother's parasol now furled against her shoulder, the boy waist-deep in grass with his arms full. Between the two pairs runs an invisible diagonal path, and the eye takes it without being asked. The figures are Camille, Monet's first wife, and Jean, their eldest son, the family he painted constantly in these years.

What scandalised contemporaries — and what the picture is loved for now — is the poppies themselves. Close to, they are only touches of vermilion, some of them absurdly large, floating free of any stem; the nearer the flower, the bigger and looser the dab, until botany dissolves into pure vibration of red against green. Monet showed the painting in April 1874 at the first exhibition of the Société anonyme des artistes in Nadar's old studio on the boulevard des Capucines — the exhibition a mocking critic named 'impressionist' after another Monet canvas. It came to the state with the great Moreau-Nélaton bequest in 1906 and hangs at the Musée d'Orsay.
